title: 37. Effects of vitamin B12 metabolites, hydroxycobalamin and adenosylcobalamin, on primary ovine satellite cells.
content:
Abstract
Cobalt (Co) is an essential micronutrient required for microbial vitamin B12 synthesis and acts as a crucial factor in energy metabolism and cell replication processes. However, Co deficiencies in pastures across the United States emphasize the need for trace mineral (TM) supplementation to address inconsistent nutrient availability and support livestock maintenance and growth. Satellite cells are essential for postnatal skeletal muscle growth in mammals, and adequate TM supplementation may improve skeletal muscle growth and overall performance. Therefore, this study investigated the effects of increasing concentrations of hydroxocobalamin (a nonphysiological form of vitamin B12) and adenosylcobalamin (a physiologically active form) on ovine satellite cell (OSC) proliferation rates and fused OSC protein synthesis rates. Primary OSC were isolated from the hind leg muscles of 9-month-old commercial hair sheep wethers (n = 3). For proliferation, cultures were grown to approximately 70% confluency, followed by treatment with 1% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and/or physiologically relevant concentrations (296 pM, 592 pM, 888 pM) of hydroxocobalamin or adenosylcobalamin. For protein synthesis, cultures were grown to approximately 80% confluency, at which point cultures were induced to differentiate and treated 48-h later with serum free media (SFM) physiologically relevant concentrations (296 pM, 592 pM, 888 pM) of hydroxocobalamin or adenosylcobalamin. Linear and quadratic contrasts were constructed to assess the effects of increasing concentrations on proliferation rates and protein synthesis rates. Proliferation rates were measured at 24-h post-treatment, and protein synthesis rates were measured at 6-h post-treatment. Increasing concentrations of adenosylcobalamin tended to quadratically (p = 0.09) increase proliferation rates of primary OSC, however adenosylcobalamin did not linearly (p = 0.13) or quadratically (p = 0.92) increase protein synthesis rates of fused OSC. Increasing concentrations of hydroxocobalamin quadratically (p = 0.01) increased proliferation rates of OSC, and linearly (p = 0.04) increased protein synthesis rates of fused OSC. Although adenosylcobalamin tended to increase proliferation rates of primary OSC, the results indicate that adenosylcobalamin alone does not sufficiently enhance protein synthesis at the doses tested. In contrast, hydroxocobalamin significantly improved satellite cell proliferation and protein synthesis and underscores its potential as a potential supplement for skeletal muscle growth. These findings provide insights into refining current trace mineral supplementation strategies to enhance skeletal muscle growth of hair sheep. Future research is warranted to evaluate supplementation strategies in live animal trials.
